item.title: Tanker hits cruise ship in New Orleans, 32 hospitalised, none critical
item.description: The cruise ship, which still had about 129 passengers and an unspecified number of crew members aboard, began to sink before tipping over, sending people into the Mississippi River ...
item.dc:creator: Bloomberg
item.content:encoded: By Cameron Fozi All passengers and crew members aboard a river cruise ship that capsized after a tanker collision in New Orleans on Friday were accounted for, with 32 people hospitalized but none critically injured, according to Mayor Helena Moreno. The Atlantic Asphalt tanker “lost control” and struck the American Heritage, operated by American Cruise Lines, around 12:30 p.m. at the Port of New Orleans, Moreno said at a news briefing. The cruise ship, which still had about 129 passengers and an unspecified number of crew members aboard, began to sink before tipping over, sending people into the Mississippi River. Harbor police were the first to respond, entering the water to pull people to safety as firefighters extended ladders from the dock. Volunteer crews in their own vessels also joined the rescue effort, Moreno said. “At this moment, the information that we have, we have zero people unaccounted for,” Moreno said. “Which truly is a miracle on the Mississippi.” Video of the incident aired by local television station WDSU, an NBC affiliate, showed a larger tanker approaching the docked cruise ship before the two vessels collided at what appeared to be a relatively slow speed. Later footage showed the American Heritage partly submerged in the river. The American Cruise Lines website describes the American Heritage as a classic paddlewheeler river boat with capacity for as many as 180 passengers, which was last renovated in 2022. “American Cruise Lines can confirm that our riverboat, American Heritage, was involved in a collision while it was docked in New Orleans,” the company said in a statement. “We are in close coordination with the US Coast Guard and local authorities. Guests and crew were evacuated, and we are deeply concerned for everyone involved.” Earlier on Friday, Louisiana Governor Jeff Landry said he was heading to New Orleans. “We are aware of the incident on the Mississippi and we are in close contact with local officials and law enforcement,” Landry said in a post on X. “I am headed to New Orleans now.”

item.title: Tata Sons listing will change 'Tata way', will engage with regulators: Noel
item.description: Noel said while 'some people' are proposing a listing for group's holding company, he fears that enlarging the number of shareholders after a listing will shift its focus to profits from philanthropy ...
item.content:encoded:
Home / Companies / News / Tata Sons listing will change 'Tata way', will engage with regulators: Noel

Tata Sons listing will change 'Tata way', will engage with regulators: Noel Noel said while 'some people' are proposing a listing for group's holding company, he fears that enlarging the number of shareholders after a listing will shift its focus to profits from philanthropy

The comments come at a time when ruptures at the top echelons of the country's largest conglomerate are out in the open | Image: Bloomberg

Press Trust of India New Delhi 3 min read Last Updated : Nov 14 2026 | 2:55 PM IST

Listen to This Article

Tata Trusts Chairman Noel Tata on Saturday said that listing Tata Sons will "fundamentally change" the over 150-year-old group's way of working and stressed that its largest owner will play a "constructive role" in engaging with the regulators to retain the conglomerate's unlisted character. Speaking at the Hindustan Times Leadership Summit here, Noel said while "some people" are proposing a listing for the group's holding company, he fears that enlarging the number of shareholders after a listing will shift its focus to profits from philanthropy. "My worry is that listing, which is what some people are proposing, will change the Tata way. And one day, if we have 30,000-40,000 shareholders, profit may take precedence over philanthropy. And I think that will fundamentally change the Tata way of working," Noel, who turned 70 on Friday, was quoted as saying.

"Tata Trusts will play a constructive role with regulators and others to try and find a solution which keeps the Tata way the way it is," he added. The 'Tata way' represents continuity, the half-brother of Ratan Tata who took over the reins of Tata Trusts after the death of the group's more charismatic leader, said, adding that an owner cannot die, retire or be bought in the model. Also Read

Who is Sunil D'Souza, the new Voltas Chairman succeeding Noel Tata?

The comments come at a time when ruptures at the top echelons of the country's largest conglomerate are out in the open, with Noel-led Tata Trusts, which owns two-thirds stake in the holding company Tata Sons, opposed to a listing, while the management of Tata Sons led by chairman N Chandrasekaran says it will have to follow the law of the land and list as per the RBI's instructions.

It can be recalled that Noel also dissented against Chandrasekaran's reappointment as Tata Sons chairman at a board meet on September 17 this year. Noel, who is reported to have expressed concerns over capital allocation and returns made in bets like Air India, digital and semiconductors businesses under Chandrasekaran, also said that he is "pleased" with the firsts that the group has achieved and included the semi-conductor project, battery and electric vehicle battery that it is putting up in the list. Speaking at the HTLS, Noel said that there has not been any change in the strategic direction of the group in terms of governance and added that discipline is needed to execute very large projects.

"Philanthropy on one hand. Nation building on other. This is independence of leadership and personalities and this will continue. I do not question the direction of what we have done. I question, sometimes, the delivery of what we are doing," Noel said. He said the Westside business was the country's first direct to consumer business by opting for private labels, where it owns the entire chain right from the fabric to the store in which the finished product is sold. Consumption has skyrocketed in the country over the past decade, he said, adding that Westside now boasts of 320 stores and is looking to see when it can touch 500.

"'While we the team (at Westside) has done a fantastic job in addressing the opportunity, I think full credit has to go to the economy, to India, the way consumption is growing is incredible," he said. He also recalled starting of Trent, and claimed that Tatas were the "pioneers of retail" in the country. The brand 'Zudio' was launched to cater to the bottom of the pyramid, he said, stressing that the price points of products remain the same even a decade later.

item.title: PM Modi summons telecom secretary over fake court orders to block sites
item.description: The findings have triggered one criminal investigation by state police against unknown persons for forgery and cheating ...
item.content:encoded:
Home / Industry / News / PM Modi summons telecom secretary over fake court orders to block sites

PM Modi summons telecom secretary over fake court orders to block sites The findings have triggered one criminal investigation by state police against unknown persons for forgery and cheating

The findings have triggered one criminal investigation by state police against unknown persons for forgery and cheating | Image: Reuters

Reuters NEW DELHI 2 min read Last Updated : Nov 14 2026 | 1:54 PM IST

Listen to This Article

Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi's office summoned the telecommunications secretary on Saturday to explain how officials ordered the takedown of more than 100 websites based on court orders that Reuters revealed were fake, two government sources said.   The intervention from Modi's office signals intensifying scrutiny after Reuters revealed on Wednesday that telecom officials directed internet providers to block 129 illegal betting websites based on fake High Court orders which were emailed to officials by people posing as lawyers.   While online betting is illegal in India, the case has raised concerns that a lack of safeguards in India's content-takedown system could allow falsified court documents to be used to block legitimate websites.     The findings have triggered one criminal investigation by state police against unknown persons for forgery and cheating.   Modi's office summoned Telecom Secretary Amit Agrawal to appear and explain the lapse, cutting short Agrawal's trip to another state, said the two government officials with knowledge of the matter. Also Read

PM Modi pays tribute to Jawaharlal Nehru on his 137th birth anniversary

Trai bars 124,000 mobile connections in spam crackdown during July-Sep

Decade-long efforts averted energy crisis during war: PM Narendra Modi

Youth launching rockets, satellites after we opened space sector: PM Modi

PM Modi inaugurates Bengaluru Metro's Pink Line, travels with CM Shivakumar

Agrawal is the most senior bureaucrat in the telecommunications ministry, which oversees everyone from big telecom operators to internet providers.   "The action taken by the Department of Telecommunications against betting accounts was carried out through the relevant field officers," said one of the people.   Agrawal and his ministry did not respond to Reuters queries, and neither did Modi's office.   Court precedents generated using AI have caused concerns among judges the world over. India's Supreme Court in July set aside a tribunal's orders that relied on non-existent judgments, and a US judge recently disqualified lawyers over use of fabricated legal citations.   On Friday, Reuters reported that the telecoms ministry had initiated an internal investigation into the alleged fraud, while police have sought ministry records as part of a criminal investigation.   The two state court orders Reuters revealed were fake, based on comments from police and the court registry, contained fabricated court logos and seals, as well as a fake QR code.   They were for months available publicly on the Department of Telecommunications' website, along with correspondence that showed government officials ordering internet providers to remove the websites.   On Saturday, one of the fake court orders was still accessible on the government's website, while one had been removed.

item.title: With shifting Iran rhetoric, Trump leaves W Asia in limbo about path ahead
item.description: President Donald Trump has had a lot to say about his thinking on the way ahead in the Iran war since Republicans were trounced in last week's midterm elections.
item.content:encoded:
Home / World News / With shifting Iran rhetoric, Trump leaves W Asia in limbo about path ahead

With shifting Iran rhetoric, Trump leaves W Asia in limbo about path ahead Trump acknowledged on the day after the midterms that the war and the global economic tumult it's caused were partly to blame for Republicans' electoral losses

US President Donald Trump | Image: Bloomberg

AP Washington 7 min read Last Updated : Nov 14 2026 | 12:29 PM IST

Listen to This Article

President Donald Trump has had a lot to say about his thinking on the way ahead in the Iran war since Republicans were trounced in last week's midterm elections. In exchanges with reporters, broadcast interviews and social media posts since Election Day, he's somehow managed to back away from carrying out additional strikes while also backing away from the prospect of additional talks with the Islamic Republic's negotiators on ending the 8-month-old conflict. The president acknowledged on the day after the midterms that the war and the global economic tumult it's caused were partly to blame for Republicans' electoral losses, while maintaining it was the right thing to do.

Then, at the start of this week, he huddled with Qatar's prime minister at the White House and afterwards told reporters that he believed it was highly unlikely he'd need to order new major strikes on Iran, declaring that the war "militarily is effectively over."   But by Thursday, he was again raising questions about whether he needed to rush to find an endgame. He declared that the US no longer needs a deal with Tehran and brusquely directed Vice President JD Vance -- who served as his chief negotiator in earlier peace talks with Iran -- to shift his attention to the administration's domestic anti-fraud campaign.

All the while, Trump warned Iran that the US military is "locked and loaded" and keeping an eye on Pickaxe Mountain, a facility linked to Iran's nuclear programme, for signs of activity. Also Read

Trump unlikely to raise Alice Huang case with China's Xi during APEC summit

Trump, Xi, Putin plan an unprecedented joint meeting on sidelines of APEC

Nvidia crisis: Senate panel summons Jensen Huang, Howard Lutnick to testify

World oil market is returning to surplus as Gulf exports recover, says IEA

India-US deal may be inked after Washington settles its tariff framework premium

"If something does not work out, I would not hesitate to act, Trump told conservative broadcaster Hugh Hewitt on Thursday. Iran war will shadow Trump during his trip to Asia Trump's tonal shifts have only added to the uncertainty about what comes next in a war in which America's allies were not consulted before it was started but nonetheless struggle to deal with its economic ramifications. "President Trump is now acting like an arsonist who has set ablaze our foreign policy," Democratic Sen. Cory Booker of New Jersey said in an interview Friday on the sidelines of the Democrats' post-election gathering in Denver. "And now he just wants to walk away."   The president's ambiguous positioning on the war is expected to loom large during a visit next week to the Philippines and the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation meetings in the Chinese tech hub of Shenzhen.

While in Shenzhen, Trump will hold an unprecedented three-way summit with China's Xi Jinping and Russia's Vladimir Putin. Trump is expected to discuss Iran and the three powers' nuclear stockpiles with Xi and Putin. The White House declined to comment directly on queries about Trump's post-election rhetoric on Iran. But Secretary of State Marco Rubio underscored that Trump's approach is leading to the Iranian economy collapsing. "The economic pain that we are inflicting on that regime is so great that there's no need for military action because we've weakened them so much," Rubio said in a Friday evening speech to the Federalist Society.

West Asia diplomats try to make sense of Trump's position Chief mediator Qatar continues to try to negotiate an interim agreement that would restore traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, a vital passageway for the flow of oil and natural gas from the Persian Gulf to global markets, while leaving open options for further discussions between the US and Iran. But those efforts are now clouded by uncertainty following Trump's shifting -- and sometimes contradictory -- comments, according to two West Asia diplomats familiar with the process. The diplomats, who spoke on condition of anonymity due to the sensitivity of the matter, said the situation had appeared to be on the right track earlier this week after Qatar's prime minister met with Trump.

But Trump's social media post Thursday declaring that the US doesn't need a deal with Iran and directing Vance "to focus his complete and total attention" on his anti-fraud campaign has created a sense of limbo. One of the diplomats said the post raised questions about why Trump appeared to be sidelining Vance, who was sceptical about launching the war but ultimately supported Trump. Trump's post came as Vance had been weighing a possible reengagement with senior Iranian negotiators, according to a person familiar with the matter who was not authorised to comment publicly and spoke on the condition of anonymity. The president posted his message calling on Vance to steer away from Iran negotiations the morning after The Wall Street Journal reported Vance was thinking about resuming talks. Trump -- who had been aware of Vance's deliberations -- believed the Iranians weren't acting in good faith, the person added.

Trump is also increasingly confident that he can credibly declare that he's achieved his military objectives in the war. But traversing the Strait of Hormuz remains treacherous. The United Nations reports October had the highest number of incidents against commercial ships in the contested waters since February. Still, Trump believes that with oil shipments through the strait reaching near-prewar levels, he could potentially leave it to Gulf countries to negotiate a deal with the Iranians on governing the critical waterway, the person said. The other regional diplomat described the push for peace as falling into a holding pattern as people await clarification from the White House on Trump's intentions.

That diplomat added it was not entirely clear to mediators or the Iranians if Trump's comments meant he was abandoning a negotiated agreement or was just posturing after the congressional midterm elections that cost his Republican Party control of Congress. Rubio insists the US hasn't given up on mediation efforts Iran remains unwilling to engage in negotiations over its nuclear programme until the US agrees to several core conditions that Iran has been demanding be part of any ceasefire agreement. Differences with Iran over its nuclear activities remain the thorniest issue, and one that Trump insists must be resolved as part of any deal meant to end the war.

Tehran's rhetoric has hardly cooled. Iran's deputy UN ambassador Gholamhossein Darzi told the United Nations Security Council on Friday that Iran "has never closed the door to diplomacy." But he warned that should the US or Israel return to bombing, his country would offer "an immediate and decisive response."   Rubio earlier this week stressed that the US is not opposed to mediators continuing their efforts. "If there's a deal to be done, the president will be the first one to be in favour of it," Rubio said. "But it's not going to be a stupid deal. It's not going to be a bad deal."   Michael Singh, managing director at the Washington Institute for Near East Policy, said he expects the status quo to persist for some time, with the US and Iran locked in a stalemate over the Strait of Hormuz and the US continuing its month-long naval blockade that's curbing the flow of Iranian crude to the global market.

Singh said the American strategy of squeezing Iran economically is a far more attractive option for Trump than military escalation or making concessions to Tehran. He also suggested Trump could always reverse his position on Vance engaging with Iranians if the president finds the Iranians are ready to seriously negotiate. "It's probably the most sensible path as well to sort of be patient, keep the pressure on, allow the mediators to keep doing their work," said Singh, who worked on West Asia issues in former President George W. Bush's White House. "And when the time is right, but not before then, is when you want to engage senior officials like the vice president and so forth.

(Only the headline and picture of this report may have been reworked by the Business Standard staff; the rest of the content is auto-generated from a syndicated feed.)
